newsitem.title: TAIWAN: New law paves way for first Taiwan futures market.
newsitem.headline: New law paves way for first Taiwan futures market.

text.p: Taiwan's parliament on Tuesday adopted a long-delayed Futures Trading Law, clearing the way to open the island's first futures exchange as soon as October.
Parliamentary bickering over the draft law during 1996 and into 1997 had forced authorities to push back the exchange's planned launch to early 1998 at the earliest.
Legislators who pushed the law through said they hoped to get an exchange up and running as early as September.

"We passed the Futures Trading Law and we want to see the finance ministry authorise establishment of an exchange house within six months," legislator Lin Chung-cheng told Reuters by telephone moments after the bill was passed.
Government officials hailed the law's passage, but cautioned that opening of a futures exchange even by October 1997 would require extensive further work.

"The exchange could open as early as October, but we need much more detailed regulation to ensure smooth operation and prevent potential financial irregularities," Securities and Exchange Commission official Lee Chi-hsien told Reuters.
Commission officials expect the first item to be traded on the new exchange would be contracts linked to the benchmark TAIEX index of the island's main Taiwan Stock Exchange.

Such contracts would offer the first domestic alternative to unauthorised offshore Taiwan stock index futures launched on January 9 by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange and the Singapore International Monetary Exchange, or SIMEX.

Analysts say pressure from offshore rivals helped prompt lawmakers to resolve deep differences over three drafts of the law to prevent local investors from turning to the CME and SIMEX contracts for a stock market hedge.
Officials said Taiwan's version of the stock index futures would be closely tailored to domestic investors' needs.
"We can design our index futures contracts to target local investors," vice finance minister Wu Chia-sheng told reporters.
The stock index futures would be followed by the launch of commodity-related contracts linked to Taiwan's voracious appetite for soybeans, corn and wheat trades, officials said.
Trading of financial futures tied to interest rates and bond yields would require central bank's approval, they said.

Taiwan futures houses already are allowed to offer a wide range of major overseas futures contracts, but to date the CME and SIMEX futures were the only contracts linked directly to Taiwan's economy. San Francisco's Pacific Stock Exchange has offered Taiwan stock-index options since January 9.
Taipei still forbids local investors to trade through local futures brokerage houses despite huge pressure before and since their launch to open up access.
Many local investors are believed to be skirting the ban by placing orders through offshore brokers, a practice that has compounded pressure to offer a domestic alternative.
The central bank hinted on Saturday that it might be willing to lift the ban, saying it would "cautiously support" allowing Taiwan investors to trade the CME, SIMEX and Pacific contracts.
No final decision had been taken, officials said.
Analysts have cautioned that a mandatory six-month government review would delay legal access to the offshore contracts.
Taiwan's government traditionally has been leery of futures, regarding them as a high-risk financial instruments all but indistinguishable from gambling.
Lawmaker Lin said he viewed the establishment of a local futures exchange as an aid to Taiwan's financial markets' development -- not a place to gamble.
"Its true that people can gamble in the futures market, but they can gamble anywhere -- even on baseball games," Lin said.
